title: Comparing: kuliko, zaidi, and adjectives that don't change
goal: Compare two options, say which is the most, and use the words for "many", "few", "other" and "all", which all agree with their noun class.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ndege au meli?
dialogs.intro: Budi plans to cross over to Zanzibar and can't decide how. Amina, who has made the trip dozens of times, has an opinion.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Nataka kwenda Zanzibar. Nichague ndege au meli?
lines.id: I want to go to Zanzibar. Should I take the plane or the ferry?
lines.literal: I-want to-go Zanzibar. I-should-choose plane or ship?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Meli ni rahisi kuliko ndege, lakini ni polepole zaidi.
lines.id: The ferry is cheaper than the plane, but slower.
lines.literal: ship is cheap than plane, but is slow more.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: How long does the ferry take?

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Saa mbili. Ndege inachukua dakika ishirini tu.
lines.id: Two hours. The plane takes only twenty minutes.
lines.literal: hours two. plane it-is-taking minutes twenty only.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Mara tatu zaidi ya meli. Tiketi ni ghali sana.
lines.id: Three times the ferry. The ticket is very expensive.
lines.literal: times three more than ship. ticket is expensive very.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Basi nitachukua meli. Nina muda mwingi, pesa chache!
lines.id: Then I'll take the ferry. I have lots of time and little money!
lines.literal: in-that-case I-will-take ship. I-have time much, money little!

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Uamuzi mzuri! Meli ya asubuhi ni bora kuliko ya jioni.
lines.id: Good decision! The morning ferry is better than the afternoon one.
lines.literal: decision good! ship of morning is better than of afternoon.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Bahari ni shwari zaidi asubuhi. Jioni kuna mawimbi makubwa.
lines.id: The sea is calmer in the morning. In the afternoon there are big waves.
lines.literal: sea is calm more morning. afternoon there-are waves big-big.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Asante! Wewe ni rafiki bora kuliko wote.
lines.id: Thanks! You're the best friend of all.
lines.literal: thanks! you are friend best than all.

lines.speaker: Amina:
lines.text: Haya, usinisifu sana! Nunua tiketi leo, si kesho.
lines.id: Oh, stop, don't flatter me! Buy the ticket today, not tomorrow.
lines.literal: enough, don't-you-me-praise too-much! buy ticket today, not tomorrow.

notes: **Kiasi gani? means "how much?" as in degree.** *Kiasi* itself means extent, measure, approximately. *Kiasi gani?* asks how far along a scale: how expensive, how far, how much. Its cousins: *Muda gani?* (how long?) and *Umbali gani?* (how far?).

**Basi has two completely different meanings.** As a noun it's "bus"; as a conjunction it's "in that case; all right then". *Basi twende!* = all right, let's go. *Haya basi* = fine, then. Context tells them apart without trouble.
**Bora means both "better" and "best"**, and as a loanword it never changes form. *Ni bora* (it's better), *bora kuliko wote* (best of all), *Ni bora tuende sasa* (we'd better go now).

**Shwari means calm, especially for the sea and the weather.** For a calm person use *mtulivu*; *shwari* can also describe a peaceful atmosphere. *Bahari ni shwari* is a sentence you'll hear a lot before a crossing — and the one you most want to hear.
**Si kesho at the end of a sentence means "not tomorrow".** It's the same *si* as in unit 1, used to deny anything that isn't a verb: *si mimi* (not me), *si sasa* (not now), *si mbali* (not far).

grammars.title: Kuliko and zaidi: more, than, most
body: Swahili **doesn't change the adjective** to compare — there's no *big → bigger* like in English. Instead you add a separate word.

head: Pattern
Example
Meaning
rows: The ferry is cheaper than the plane.
He/She is the nicest of all.
The price is the same as yesterday.
This one is different from that one.

after: *Kuliko* literally means "than what there is" — a frozen form of the verb *kuwa*. It never changes, works for any noun class, and always stands between the two things compared.

**For "the most"**, Swahili has no special form. Instead: *kuliko wote* (than everyone), *kuliko zote* (than all N-class things), *kuliko vyote*, and so on — the *-ote* form follows the class of the thing compared. Alternatives: *bora zaidi* (the best) and *namba moja* (number one, colloquial).

The adjectives most often compared: *kubwa* (big), *dogo* (small), *ghali* (expensive), *rahisi* (cheap), *nzuri* (good), *mbaya* (bad), *refu* (long), *fupi* (short), *haraka* (fast), *polepole* (slow), *tamu* (tasty), *bora* (good, better).

grammars.title: Many, few, other, all
body: These four quantity words all start with a bare stem, so all four follow their noun class — and the sounds change enough that they feel like different words. This table sorts it out.
after: Singular forms for "other": *mtu mwingine* (another person), *kitu kingine* (another thing), *nyumba nyingine* (another house), *gari lingine* (another car), *mti mwingine* (another tree). Note that *-ingi* (many) is almost always plural, while *-ingine* (other) is used in both numbers.

Everyday phrases: *watu wengi* (many people), *pesa nyingi* (a lot of money), *muda mwingi* (a lot of time), *maji mengi* (a lot of water), *siku chache* (a few days), *mara nyingine* (another time), *kila mtu* (everyone).
⚠️ Don't mix up *wengi* (many people) and *wengine* (other people) — one syllable separates "many people came" from "other people came". Listen for the *-ne* at the end.

blocks.text: Sentences you'll need at the terminal: *Basi la Arusha linaondoka saa ngapi?* (what time does the bus to Arusha leave?), *Nauli ni ngapi?* (how much is the fare?), *Kuna nafasi?* (is there room?), *Nataka tiketi mbili* (I want two tickets).

The verbs: *kupanda* (to board), *kushuka* (to get off), *kuondoka* (to depart), *kufika* (to arrive), *kuchelewa* (to be late), *kukosa* (to miss). *Nimekosa basi* = I've missed the bus — a sentence you'll need sooner or later.

sections.title: Paired adjectives — one read, two words

blocks.text: The fastest way to add adjectives is to learn them in pairs. The left and right columns are opposites.

Notice the hyphen before some words: it marks words that **agree with their noun class**. Those without a hyphen — *safi*, *chafu*, *ghali*, *rahisi*, *gumu*, *hodari*, *kuukuu*, *joto*, *baridi* — are loanwords that never change form, which means nine adjectives you don't have to worry about at all.

*Kali* has the widest range of any of them: *jua kali* (blazing sun), *mwalimu mkali* (a strict teacher), *pilipili kali* (hot chili), *sabuni kali* (harsh soap). And on the streets of Tanzania, *jua kali* is also the name for workshops and small businesses that work outdoors — literally "under the blazing sun".

exercises.prompt: Compare with kuliko. Example: meli + rahisi + ndege → Meli ni rahisi kuliko ndege.

items: The ferry is cheaper than the plane.
He/She is the best friend of all.
I have a lot of time, little money.
The price is the same as yesterday.
